newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy BTPs seen rising, spread vs Bund to narrow.
newsitem.headline: Italy BTPs seen rising, spread vs Bund to narrow.

text.p: Italian debt futures may pause for breath after rallying hard and fast recently but are likely to set fresh records in coming weeks after an interest rate cut by the Bank of Italy, economists said.

The central bank's 75 basis point cut late on Tuesday on the key discount rate to 6.75 percent and the fixed term advances rate to 8.25 percent caught Italian markets off guard in terms of its timing although a reduction has been long awaited.
"Barring a big shock from the U.S. all the factors are in place for a further leg to the rally," said Robert Prior, European economist at HSBC Markets in London.
The March Btp future on LIFFE posted the latest in a line of record highs at the opening on Wednesday, hitting 132.30 before inching to 132.10 by 1425 GMT, 37 basis points up on the day.
The yield on the July 2006 Btp held at 7.22 percent and the spread over the benchmark 10-year Bund was 151 basis points, neither greatly changed from late Tuesday before the easing.
Btp futures have been outpacing the cash market in the last few days and analysts expected cash to play catch-up for now with the chance for a futures correction setting in soon.
"The March future is maybe reaching the highs for now. The near term objective is 132.50 and profit-taking could set in now," a broker at an Italian bank in London said.
With a correction over, analysts cite targets of 133-134 on the future in coming weeks while Btp-Bund spread forecasts are for below 150 basis points near term.
Luca Jellinek, bond strategist at Paribas in London, said the spread could narrow to the low 140s in the coming week.

Francesco Giordano, senior economist at San Paolo bank in London, said: "The U.S. market is positive, the German one too, the lira is strong and the climate positive. The spread between the 10-year Italian and the 10-year Bund could fall to 125 basis points in a month and a half or two months."

HSBC's Prior said a spread closing in towards 100 in the next quarter would not surprise him. "But I do think it has to reverse at some point. The fundamentals on the budgetary side are not good enough to justify that kind of spread so we'd be looking for a reversal sometime in the second half of the year."
He then saw it flaring again, even returning to 200 plus.
Darren Williams, European economist at UBS in London, also saw the spread sustained and narrowing in coming months.

"The only thing which makes one still a little concerned is that it's come in a long way and if there were to be any sort of shock on the European monetary union front things could unravel quite quickly," Williams said.

On the yield curve Jellinek said: "In theory the very short end should benefit mostly because three-years are already discounting a lot. But recent experience shows probably they'll do fairly well too -- so three-years will stay expensive."
Analysts said expectations of further Italian rate cuts would keep the market buoyed but Williams sounded a cautionary note for further out.
"It's always worth remembering Italy is the equivalent of a highly geared company -- in a low interest environment it tends to do very well," he said.
"The key turning point for high yielders is when the global interest rate environment turns. That may happen as a result of the U.S. Federal Reserve hiking rates.

"But more likely it would need the rate environment to turn in Europe for there to be a major reversal in Btps -- and that isn't going to happen at any stage in the near future," he added. --Milan bureau +392 66129507
